cells.tense: The persistence is right here in the room, and it is still working.
cells.act: persist on your own reserves through the pressure
cells.ask: Take the piece of your care that costs the most and do its next part on what you already have — no new supplies, no borrowed hands, no fresh plan. See how far your own reserves carry it.
cells.core:
You keep going on what's growing here longer than most people would, and it doesn't cost you the way it costs them. Whatever needs tending gets tended, on your own fuel, without a fuss. That's the balanced form: the reserves are there, and you're drawing on them.

So put them where it counts this week. Not everywhere — take the piece of it that costs the most and do it on what you already have: no new supplies, no borrowed hands, no plan you haven't started yet. Just your own reserves through the pressure. You'll learn how much is actually in you, and whether the thing needed all the arranging you've been giving it. Both answers are useful. Neither is a verdict on you.
cells.sheetLine: You keep it going on your own fuel.
cells.verb: keep going on what you have, long after it stopped being easy
cells.place: where you look after what is still growing

cells.tense: You will be braced for the next demand before the present one has finished.
cells.act: pause before you let it be known
cells.ask: Next time you're certain what's coming for something you tend, sit with that certainty a day before acting. Let the day pass. Then check whether it arrived before you move.
cells.core:
You look ahead at what's growing and you see what's coming — the delay, the failure, the extra demand. So you move to meet it. From where you stand, that's care; you've been right enough times that the certainty feels earned. But you're answering next month's problem with this month's hands, and the thing you tend is growing at a pace you can't set from here.

Try holding what you know a while before you act on it. Next time you're certain what's coming, sit with it a day. Let the day finish. Then check whether it actually showed up before you move. Sometimes it will have, and you'll be ready. Sometimes you'll find you were preparing for something that didn't come. Either way the instinct gets tested before it gets spent.
cells.sheetLine: You fix next season's problem before this season is over.
cells.verb: keep going on what you have, long after it stopped being easy

cells.tense: You have been standing at a door that closed behind you a while back.
cells.act: tend the resource with responsible care
cells.ask: Give one neglected thing a single plain piece of care — water it, clear a space for it, set it where light reaches. Then stop there. Nothing more is asked of you here.
cells.core:
Care is thin here. What you look after gets what's left over, and there's not much left over — you're somewhere you've mostly moved past, standing in the doorway rather than anywhere near the middle of it. It isn't that you stopped caring. The habit of care that used to run itself has gone quiet, and you're drawing on what's already spent.

Don't force it back. Take one neglected thing — not the biggest, just the one you'd notice — and give it a single plain piece of care: water it, clear the space around it, set it where the light reaches. Then stop there. Don't schedule the next one and don't grade yourself on it. Doing it once is the whole ask. Steady returns through the body before it returns anywhere else, and one honest piece of care is where that begins.
cells.sheetLine: Nothing gets much care because the caring has run dry.

cells.tense: The persistence is holding everything up, and it is the last thing you would name as yours.
cells.act: stand firm in the material hardship
cells.ask: Go over one stretch from this past year when something you look after kept going through a lean season — what it took, the mornings, the weeks. Put it somewhere you'll run into it again.
cells.core:
Things under your care keep going. Slow weeks, months when the money or the patience was thin, and still nothing dropped — you'd tell it that way if anyone asked, as if it just continued by itself. It didn't. Someone kept it going through all of it, and that got no counting, because you don't count that kind of thing.

Go back and count a stretch. Take one season from this past year when something you tend got held together — not the hardest, just a real one — and lay out what it took. The mornings. The errands. The weeks you did it anyway. Put it where you'll run into it. This isn't for a thank-you; nobody has to read it. It's for the next lean week, when you'll be doing the same thing again and could stand to know whose hands did it last time.
cells.sheetLine: Whatever you hold keeps standing, and you don't count it.
cells.verb: keep going on what you have, long after it stopped being easy
cells.place: where you look after what is still growing

attempts.check: The unsupported claim to watch: that the person has 'kept going through a lot' — the record says persistence is the signature's character, not that hardship occurred or what it was, so every cell locates the leaning and never names the events. A reader could object that some of what I call their holding is actually other people's work being done by them — I've kept every reference to others as circumstances they're tending around, not as things they've secretly authored. The asks survive being wrong: each one is a small, bounded act that teaches something about steadiness or attention even if the read missed, and none promises an outcome. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'tested many times over' — cut it; the person's own account of what they've been through outranks my sense of it.
